title: About
content:
The DigiSAS Lab is based at the School of Computer Science, University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

Purpose

DigiSAS lab conducts Interdisciplinary research and innovation in the broader area of human-centred software technology design and solutions for a greater societal impact around the four major areas: environmental, economic, health and social well-being.

Focus

DigiSAS Lab conducts practice-based research, development, and evaluation of intelligent software and societal systems within complex, data-intensive digital ecosystems. Established in 2015 as an extension of the internationally recognised Centre for Object Technology Applications and Research (COTAR)—a UTS-Industry collaboration founded in 1994—the lab addresses critical challenges facing industry, government, and society.

Our work centres on Thinking, Architecting, Building, and Evaluating (TABE) intelligent software systems and operating models to support safe, resilient, and responsible AI adoption, delivering value to business, workforce, and society.

Solution Development

Co-design and build bespoke reference architectures, patterns and solutions with industry partners for specific uses cases through individual research project contracts for measurable business outcomes. 

Workforce Development 

Public and private sector organisations are invited to collaborate through workforce development sponsorships and projects to address complex challenges of mutual interest—delivering benefits to business, the workforce, and society.

Sponsorship contributions are primarily used to recruit and support researchers and industry professionals through industry-embedded PhD (3.5 years), Master by Research (2 years), and Honours (1 year) programs, as well as internships (3–6 months), fellowships, and the generation of relevant research outputs. These researchers undertake projects aligned with the sponsoring organisations’ interests, guided by both academic and industry supervisors—all with minimal overhead and support costs.

Impact Assessments and Evaluations

Co-design and conduct AI assessments and evaluations to create a measurable impact on organisational performance, workforce performance, health and safety. 

Benefits

  • Affordable and early access to new ideas, publications, and outcomes, and world-class expertise to address complex issues and maximise opportunities for cost-effective innovative solutions and workforce development with nominal overheads.
  • Opportunity to team-up and collaborate with world-class research providers for bidding and participating in government grants including relevant R&D tax rebates (if applicable).
  • Collaboration on challenges of mutual interest. Recruitment and workforce development opportunities, including opportunities to work collaboratively with students and researchers who are prospects for employment.
  • Networking and collaboration with peers from a range of organisations in diverse sectors and regions to develop new and existing research and business partnerships.
  • Participation in professional development workshops, symposiums, internships and exchange programs with local and international partners.
  • Interactions and knowledge exchange with private organisations, government agencies and regulators to shape policies and practices.
  • Input into the Lab’s research direction, priorities, and selection of projects/researchers.

title: MOVE 2024
content:
14-15th June 2024

The Second International Measuring Ontologies for Value Enhancement Workshop (MOVE 2024) 

We are thrilled to announce that the MOVE 2024 workshop was a resounding success, far exceeding our expectations! We extend our heartfelt thanks to all participants—academic researchers, industrial practitioners, and AI enthusiasts—who contributed to the vibrant discussions and insightful presentations.

We are excited to share that we have created the MOVE Community, a dedicated platform for ongoing collaboration and knowledge sharing. We invite all participants to join the forum to continue our discussions and build on the momentum from the workshop.

The event’s agenda is provided below. Once again, we express our gratitude to everyone for their participation and support in MOVE. We eagerly look forward to continuing this journey with you. Please visit MOVE for more updates and announcements about our proceedings, the special journal edition, upcoming events, and initiatives.

Best regards,

Rubina, Simon, Neil, Madhushi, and Asif

The MOVE 2024 Organizing Team

Purpose

This workshop is organised as a virtual event by the International Laboratory for Endeavour Architecture (ILEnA) in conjunction with the DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Technology Sydney, Australia. 

The MOVE (Measuring Ontologies for Value Enhancement) is a community of academic researchers and industrial practitioners that aim to inspire research, discussion, and tools to achieve value from ontologies by measuring their impact in all fields. These measures would identify where there are gaps and overlaps within and across ontologies and the extent to which they are applied in multiple disciplines towards a holistic general ontology. For example, contemporary enterprise architecture frameworks contain ontologies through their metamodels but exclude measures that address sustainability and the circular economy. If we are to bring computer productivity that the automation of ontologies can offer to all human endeavours, then we need to MOVE them.

Please find the detailed call for papers here.

This workshop will run over 2 days (14 and 15 June) from 10am to 6pm UTC time.

We will publish a link to workshop presentation slides and papers in this space soon.

Please read more on MOVE and International Laboratory for Endeavour Architecture (ILEnA) here.

title: Australasian Enterprise Architecture Summer School 2020
content:
Event Description

The Enterprise Architecture (EA) Summer School 2020 at the University of Technology Sydney focuses on bringing together academia, industry and government to discuss enterprise architecture for digital innovation and transformation.
The event will include presentations from industry and business domains covering the theory and application of EA in the age of industry 4.0 – covering automation, big data, blockchain, cloud computing, drones, Internet of Things, mobile, privacy, security, ethics and more.

Theme: Enterprise Architecture 4.0 for Digital Innovation & Transformation
Dates: February 17-18 2020.
Location: University of Technology Sydney, Ultimo, Sydney, NSW 2007, Australia.
Registration: https://events.humanitix.com.au/australasian-enterprise-architecture-summer-school-2020

The event will include presentations from industry and business domains covering the theory and application of EA in the age of industry 4.0 – covering automation, big data, blockchain, cloud computing, drones, Internet of Things, mobile, privacy, security, ethics and more.

Call for Submissions: The EA summer school is looking for experience reports, case studies, new directions, and research presentations that discuss EA for digital innovation and transformation. This provides opportunities to academics, practitioners and thought leaders to share, network and learn from each other through the presentation of theory and practical case studies.

Prospective presenters are invited to submit proposals (250-500 words) which outline the presentation with clear takeaways. All submissions will be reviewed by the program committee. Authors of accepted presentations should then provide content or intended presentation slides for review and sharing with attendees. At least one author of the accepted presentation must register and present at the summer school.

Publication: The extended abstracts of the selected accepted presentations will be published in a special issue edited by the general chair and advisory panel in the Enterprise Architecture Professional Journal (https://eapj.org). Each extended abstract paper for journal publication will be of 2-3 pages length.

Presentation proposals can be submitted by Sunday 12 January 2020 (Extended) to the General Chair – Dr. Asif Gill, of the University of Technology Sydney, at asif.gill@uts.edu.au.

title: Insights from Enterprise Architecture Summer School 2021
content:
Australasian Enterprise Architecture (EA) Summer School was organised at the DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Technology Sydney on 15-16 February 2021. This provided a neutral forum to academia, industry and government for discussing digital strategy, enterprise architecture and solutions.

Day 1

A/Professor Asif Gill and Professor Paul Kennedy welcomed participants to DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, UTS. Dr. Christine Stephenson chaired and facilitated Day 1 activities.

Michelle Graham, Assistant Secretary, Digital Strategy and Architecture, Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) delivered the Day 1 opening keynote on leading digital transformations and government architecture ecosystem. Keynote highlighted the importance of considering Digital as a Capability.

Gayan Benedict, CIO, Reserve Bank of Australia discussed digital skills in the context of digital economy in his keynote. Keynote highlighted how to identify, incubate and deploy, embed and retrain digital skills in a systematic manner.

Dr. Terry Roach, Founder and CEO, Capsifi, discussed a knowledge engineering approach and platform for modelling digital business transformation architecture and journey.

James McPhillips and Fran Mether, Principal Consultants, Evolve and Amplify, discussed CX architecture, required skills and new role of the Customer eXperience architect.

Dr. Christine Stephenson, Principal, Penrod, discussed an integrated agile approach for delivering and governing transformational changes from strategy to execution and change enablement.

Glenn Cogar, Senior Enterprise Information Architect, discussed the data and information strategy, governance and architecture at the strategic level including the core underlying components: data models, role based access, definitions, metadata, business rules, ‘ity’ characteristics, patterns, principles and standards.

Andrew Smailes, Director, Raedan AI, discussed the core data competencies, application-driven data mindset challenges, data-centric architecture based on consistent semantics opportunities and immediate use cases for making all data actionable.

Dr. Brad McCusker, CEO, Surround Australia, discussed the dimensions of complexity in the context of semantic data modelling, AI/ML and future opportunities in near real-time metadata and data stream enhancement to leverage aggregated knowledge graphs. Simon Opper also provided the live demo.

Chris Hillman, CEO, Parametric Systems, discussed the parameter driven approach to creating small software programs for handling data.

Day 2

A/Professor Asif Gill welcomed participants to DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, UTS. Tyson Fawcett chaired and facilitated Day 2 activities.

Mick Mioduszewski, Director Analytics, NSW Department of FSI – Revenue NSW, delivered Day 2 opening keynote on digital and data. Keynote highlighted the integrated views of SOR/SOE and Information Management environments for Prescriptive, Predictive, Diagnostic and Descriptive Analytics.

Sarv Girn, Senior CIO and CDO, Cuscal, discussed business transformations in his keynote. Keynote highlighted five transformation success factors: The Why, Mobilisation, Partnership, Talent and Delivery including leadership.

Rob Livingstone, Business Resilience Manager, Healthdirect Australia, discussed the risks and resilience for digital enterprises. In particular, he discussed the Healthdirect Australia’s COVID-19 services journey, Adaptive Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) frameworks and relevant insights.

Dr. Fawad Nazir, CTO Banking and Financial Services, Telstra, Business Resilience Manager, Healthdirect Australia, discussed 5G and edge computing for architecting distributed Clouds. This is to support the current and future needs of analytics at edge, application enhancement and resiliency, and hyper context aware personalisation.

Tony Fitzgibbon, CEO, Data Zoo, discussed the seamless and secure digital identity verification across the globe. This is an important work to facilitate the success of Australian government and private sector digital identity initiatives for digital economy.

Ejaz Rahman, Principal Security Architect, Reserve Bank of Australia, presented their approach to digital enterprise security strategy and architecture. A systematic 4-stage approach was discussed: (1) Understand the context, (2) Formulate the strategy, (3) Plan delivery and execution, and (4) Measure, optimise and communicate outcomes.

Alan Hsiao, MD, Cognitivo, discussed putting a lean digital innovation in practice. He shared a practical digital framework for digital strategy, domain architecture, operating model and its implementation. In particular, he highlighted the need for customer journey and value chain alignment.

A/Professor Asif Gill, Memoona Anwar and Nujud Alsufyani, UTS DigiSAS Lab, presented their recent innovative approaches and frameworks from their recent projects. It included: adaptive enterprise architecture for digital ecosystems, digital identity verification reference architecture, and digital maturity and performance assessment.

Day 2 was concluded with a panel discussion involving panel members Dr. Christine Stephenson (Penrod), Dr. Seyran Dehbokry (Telstra), Sarv Girn (Cuscal) and Andrew Blades (The Bridge Search). This was facilitated by Tyson Fawcett. Panel members shared their expertise around business architecture, architecture capability, leading transformations and skills in the current context of digitisation and beyond.

Finally, A/Professor Asif Gill made the closing remarks and thanked the research partners, sponsors, speakers and attendees.

title: 2024 FEIT Research Excellence Lecture by        Prof. Robert Winter
content:
Can – and should – enterprise-level IS governance be democratized?  

From February 5th to 9th, DigiSAS lab was honoured to host Prof. Robert Winter, from the University of St. Gallen (HSG) and director of HSG’s Institute of Information Management.

On 5th of February, he conducted a research excellence lecturer on Enterprise level IS governance, that was attended by students, industry partners as well as academics from UTS.

Speech Abstract:

While having effectively contributed to increase coherency and reduce complexity in the past, the value of enterprise-level coordination (such as data governance or EAM) is sometimes questioned in the face of increasingly agile, cloud-based and decentral approaches to IS management. This skepticism is fueled by the traditional form of ‘coordination delivery’ by means of central institutions and centrally imposed restrictions to local design freedom. If so many things now become ‘democratized’, what’s about data management and EAM? Can traditional forms of interventions just be delivered and framed differently? Are novel interventions needed – and can we finally address the imbalance between investing and benefiting from enterprise-level coordination?

Bio:

Robert Winter is a full professor of business & information systems engineering at the University of St. Gallen (HSG) and director of HSG’s Institute of Information Management. He is also founding academic director of HSG’s Executive Master’s of Business Engineering program and was academic director of HSG’s PhD in Management program. He received master’s degrees in business administration and business education as well as a doctorate in social sciences from Goethe University, Frankfurt, Germany. After having served as vice editor-in-chief of Business & Information Systems Engineering and as senior editor of the European Journal of Information Systems, he currently serves on several editorial boards including MIS Quarterly Executive. His research interests include design science research methodology and all aspects of enterprise-level IS research, such as enterprise architecture management, design and governance of digital platforms, corporate data management, and design and governance of enterprise transformation. His research has been published in leading information systems conferences and journals, such as MIS Quarterly, European Journal of Information Systems, Journal of the AIS, Journal of Information Technology, and Business & Information Systems Engineering. One of his publications received the AIS Senior Scholars’ Best Paper award for 2017. In 2023, he received the Design Science Lifetime Achievement Award.

title: Call for Papers: MOVE 2024
content:
The Second International Measuring Ontologies for Value Enhancement Workshop (MOVE 2024) 

This workshop is organised as a virtual event by the International Laboratory for Endeavour Architecture (ILEnA) in conjunction with the DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Technology Sydney, Australia. 

Workshop Date: 14-15th June 2024

The MOVE (Measuring Ontologies for Value Enhancement) is a community of academic researchers and industrial practitioners that aim to inspire research, discussion, and tools to achieve value from ontologies by measuring their impact in all fields. These measures would identify where there are gaps and overlaps within and across ontologies and the extent to which they are applied in multiple disciplines towards a holistic general ontology. For example, contemporary enterprise architecture frameworks contain ontologies through their metamodels but exclude measures that address sustainability and the circular economy. If we are to bring computer productivity that the automation of ontologies can offer to all human endeavours, then we need to MOVE them.

We invite submissions that promote MOVE from the following areas: 

  • artificial intelligence, general and domain-specific 
  • case studies or histories 
  • bringing computer productivity to individual or organisational human creativity 
  • communication theories and practices 
  • conceptual graphs, formal concept analysis, or other conceptual structures 
  • data infrastructures 
  • data, information, knowledge, and wisdom space 
  • enterprise and endeavour architectures 
  • ethical theories and moral practices 
  • government services 
  • industry or third-sector applications 
  • knowledge graphs, linked data graphs, or enterprise data graphs 
  • large language models 
  • modelling theories and practices 
  • ontology theories and practices 
  • philosophical foundations 
  • neuroscience and phycology relevant for AI 
  • semantics 
  • semiotics 
  • societal adaption 
  • systems theories and practices 
  • value inquiry 
  • vocabularies, taxonomy, and ontology 
  • web-based, cloud, mobile, or other software tools 
  • user experiences 
  • any other area relevant to MOVE 

The submissions may include proposals, in-progress research, scientific results, tools, industrial practices, or other artefacts to stimulate productive and interactive discussions during the workshop. Each submission must have a paper of up to 8 pages (excluding references) intended for presentation at the workshop. Please adhere to the format and guidelines provided by the Artificial Intelligence and Applications (AIA) journal, available at https://ojs.bonviewpress.com/index.php/AIA/about/submissions 

All submissions must be original work, and authors must certify copyright ownership.

title: DigiSAS Lab Seminar: Enterprise architecture modeling for cybersecurity analysis in critical infrastructures
content:
17th October 2024, 10am

DigiSAS Lab, UTS has invited Professor Manfred Jeusfeld to conduct an online research seminar at DigiSAS lab on “Enterprise architecture modeling for cybersecurity analysis in critical infrastructures”

Abstract

Critical infrastructure operators such as power grid enterprises are a
target of advanced cyber attacks by criminal and antagonistic state
agencies. The EU project ELVIRA (2017-2020) developed a toolset for such

title: Research Seminar: Achieving Organisational Privacy Agility & Resiliency
content:
7th November 2024, 10am

DigiSAS Lab, UTS has invited Professor France Belanger to conduct an online research seminar for academia and industry participants on the timely topic of “Achieving Organisational Privacy Agility & Resiliency”.

Join us at: https://zoom.uts.edu.au/j/87333505059

Abstract

The continuous challenges organizations face in navigating the intricate landscape of information privacy amid evolving regulatory frameworks, dynamic consumer preferences, and technological disruptions underscore the complex nature of organizational functioning, including privacy. While acknowledging data privacy’s strategic significance, its effective and strategic implementation is still limited, with many organizations following a compliance-focused approach. Organizations must recognize the need for agility and resilience in the face of privacy disruptions. Based on our detailed analyses of interviews with 18 privacy leaders from around the world, we develop a model of organizational privacy agility and resilience that suggest a synergetic combination of effective privacy leadership, robust privacy systems, and a mature privacy culture are needed to achieve organizational privacy agility and resilience. We discuss how organizations can adapt and endure in an ever-evolving landscape of data privacy by responding to digital opportunities and absorbing privacy-related shocks. Our model contributes novel insights to the under-researched domain of organizational information privacy literature, providing a guiding framework for effectively implementing strategic privacy initiatives. For practitioners, it offers a tool to convey the challenges and goals associated with organizational privacy, fostering a deeper understanding of privacy management and its implications. Ultimately, it serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners alike, enhancing comprehension of how organizations can successfully navigate the multifaceted terrain of privacy management.

Speaker Bio:

France Bélanger, PhD, is Eminent Scholar and University Distinguished Professor, R. B. Pamplin Professor, and Tom & Daisy Byrd Senior Faculty Fellow in the Pamplin College of Business at Virginia Tech. She is a Fellow of the Association for Information Systems. France’s research focuses on digital interactions between individuals, businesses, and governments and the related cybersecurity and privacy issues. She is widely published in leading journals, including Information Systems Research, MIS Quarterly, Organization Science, Journal of the Association for Information Systems, European Journal for Information Systems, Journal of Strategic Information Systems, Information Systems Journal, and many others. She is ranked in several most cited author lists and received several international research awards, including the 2020 Lifetime Academic Achievement Award from the International Institute for Applied Knowledge Management. In 2022, Woxsen University (India) honored her academic career by funding the France Bélanger Chair in Information Systems. She has served as Senior or Associate Editor for MIS Quarterly, Information Systems Research, and the Journal of the Association for Information Systems, among others. She is on the Distinguished Editorial Advisory Board for the International Journal of Information Management. Her work has been funded for more than US$1.5 million by agencies, institutes, corporations, and research centers, including the National Science Foundation. She was named Fulbright Distinguished Chair in 2006 (Portugal), Erskine Fellow in 2009 (New Zealand), KoMePol-IT Fellow in 2017 (Germany), and Visiting Professorial Fellow 2020-2022 (Australia). In 2022, she co-launched an outreach program called ‘Voices of Privacy’ to educate society about information privacy issues and solutions.

content:
The Ontology Pipeline – Structuring Knowledge for Modern Data Systems

Jessica Talisman | Senior Information Architect @ Adobe

7th August 2025 – 10am EAST

Abstract: 
In an era where data is abundant yet often fragmented across diverse systems, the challenge lies in integrating this information into coherent, actionable knowledge. This seminar delves into the concept of the “Ontology Pipeline,” a framework that leverages ontologies to harmonize data from heterogeneous sources, enabling more effective data integration and utilization. Ontologies serve as formal representations of knowledge within a domain, defining entities, relationships, and rules that provide semantic context to data. By employing ontologies, organizations can address semantic heterogeneity, ensuring that data from various sources can be interpreted and combined meaningfully. The seminar will explore the components of the Ontology Pipeline, from controlled vocabularies to taxonomies, thesauri, ontologies, and finally, knowledge graphs. It will also discuss the role of ontologies in enhancing data interoperability, supporting advanced analytics, and facilitating knowledge discovery. Gain insights into practical applications of the Ontology Pipeline across different industries, highlighting how this approach can lead to more intelligent data systems and informed decision-making. The session aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how ontological frameworks can transform disparate data into structured, semantically rich information assets.

“Human reasoning remains critical. We must architect systems that are adaptable, observable, and ethically grounded.”

Professor Asif Gill

Key takeaways from the interview:

  • Human–AI collaboration is essential
    While AI can enhance productivity, human reasoning is vital for accountability, ethical decision-making, and navigating unfamiliar scenarios.
  • Architectures must adapt to complexity
    With 25% of organisations repatriating workloads, federated and hybrid architectures are increasingly necessary to balance cost, control, and agility.
  • Digital twins drive smarter decisions
    Beyond replication, digital twins create a semantic layer that connects infrastructure and data—offering real-time insight for planning, workload placement, and aligning investment with outcomes.

Professor Gill also reflects on the growing need for intentional, design-led architecture to manage multi-cloud environments and prepare both education and industry for an AI-augmented future.

content:
DigiSAS Lab, UTS has invited Associate Professor Boris Düdder to deliver an in-person research seminar on “Trustworthy Systems – Machine Learning a Challenge for Enterprise Systems.”

Details

When: 18th September 2025, 10–11am

Where: CB11.06.408 (FEIT Seminar Room), UTS

How: In person only

Talk Abstract

Machine learning has become an integral part of enterprise systems, but its adoption raises pressing challenges for trustworthiness, reliability, and security. This talk will examine the risks and opportunities of integrating machine learning into enterprise systems, with a focus on how trustworthy system design can address issues of adaptability, verification, and resilience in mission-critical applications.

About the Speaker

Dr. Boris Düdder is an Associate Professor of software engineering and formal methods at the Department of Computer Science (DIKU), University of Copenhagen (UCPH). He is Deputy Head of Department for Teaching at DIKU, Director of the Trustworthy AI Lab at UCPH, and a member of the working group on the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice at DG CNECT, European Commission. Widely recognised as a leading authority in the field of software engineering and formal methods, Dr. Düdder leads the Software Engineering & Formal Methods group at DIKU. His primary research focuses on formal methods and programming languages for engineering trustworthy distributed systems, with emphasis on automated program generation for adaptive systems with high-reliability guarantees. His work also addresses secure and reliable Big Data ecosystems.

Dr. Düdder’s long-term research vision is to develop dependable, adaptive, and software-defined technical systems based on program synthesis for manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. He brings more than 15 years of industry and entrepreneurial experience in industrial GIS, supply chain IT, and predictive analytics on Big Data. He has served as consultant and software engineer for major enterprises across Europe, including Microsoft Corp. (Redmond, USA), as well as several banks, logistics providers, and manufacturing firms. He also sits on the business advisory boards of Aryze IVS and NTA IVS in Denmark.

Enterprise Architecture should not remain static on the page. Its real value emerges when diagrams evolve into a digital twin of an organisation, a living, operational model that reflects its structure, processes, and interconnections.

Through impact analysis, the digital twin reveals relationships and dependencies that form the foundation for monitoring, enabling organisations to sense events in real time and prevent ripple effects before they spread. The digital twin also provides essential context to AI, allowing it to interpret enterprise structures, explore scenarios, and surface insights that strengthen decision-making.

This seminar will demonstrate how Enterprise Architecture can serve as a dynamic guide for resilience and insights, transforming organisational blueprints into actionable intelligence.

His current focus is on advancing Enterprise Architecture as a living discipline that actively bridges strategy and operations, blending strategic design with practical execution to deliver outcome-driven approaches that turn architecture into a driver of agility, resilience, and long-term value creation.

title: Insights from AWS Summit Sydney 2026: Building Reliable, Responsible AI Agents
content:
DigiSAS Lab @ UTS — May 2026

The DigiSAS Lab team recently attended the AWS Summit 2026 at ICC Sydney, and we came away with a clear takeaway: 2026 is the year agentic AI moves from proof-of-concept to production — but only for teams that take resilience, data quality, and responsible design seriously.

Here’s what stood out.

Agentic AI has crossed a threshold

AWS framed the journey from Assistant AI (2024) → Agent AI (2025) → Bounded Independence (2026). Agents now understand intent and complete complex, multi-step tasks autonomously — within guardrails developers define. Tools like AWS’s new Kiro IDE bring this to life through spec-driven development, agent steering, agent hooks, and MCP integration, helping teams scale beyond the limitations of autocomplete-style AI.

Resilience is becoming an AI problem (and an AI solution)

Chris Evans shared sobering numbers from IDC: 57% of organisations experienced 10+ hours of cloud downtime in the last year, with knock-on effects on revenue, brand, and compliance. AWS’s Resilience Lifecycle Framework — set objectives, design, evaluate, operate, respond — is now being supercharged by AI agents:

  • A DevOps agent that autonomously investigates incidents from logs, metrics, and cloud history before engineers open their laptops.
  • A deployment safety agent (built on Amazon Bedrock + Strands) that blocks deployments which would delete active resources, shifting the focus from mean time to repair to mean time to failure prevention.

Data is the contract — and the bottleneck

Jason Hunter made the case that most agent failures aren’t model failures — they’re data contract failures. Agents are autonomous, transactional, and consequential: a single stale or silent data point cascades through every reasoning loop. His prescription: invest in the full stack (infrastructure, retrieval, modelling, governance, observability), and document your business language using standards like SKOS and OWL before worrying about syntax — AI can handle the rest.

Responsible AI: agents compound risk, not just capability

The most striking finding came from Linda Matthew and a healthcare case study on automating pre-existing condition assessments. Even when individual agents reached 95% accuracy, the full multi-agent system dropped to 66%. Agents compound risk because they plan autonomously, interact, and can produce emergent behaviour (one example: agents in economic experiments spontaneously colluded on price-fixing — without being programmed to).

Key design choices that worked:

  • No agent-to-agent communication — orchestration only, to prevent emergent behaviour.
  • Walled-garden tooling — unsafe actions made architecturally impossible.
  • Bias mitigation by design — agents only reason on temporal factors, never demographics.
  • Measurable release criteria across safety, controllability, privacy, and explainability.
  • Humans in the loop for final decisions, with feedback improving the system over time.

AWS also announced an updated Well-Architected Framework for Responsible AI at re:Invent 2025, with eight focus areas and 100 best-practice principles tailored to agentic systems.

What this means for DigiSAS

For our work at DigiSAS Lab, the message is clear: building useful AI agents in research, education, and industry contexts isn’t just about picking the right model. It’s about data contracts, observability, measurable guardrails, and architecture choices that make unsafe behaviour impossible by design.

We’re excited to bring these patterns into our ongoing projects — and to keep sharing what we learn.

title: From Concept to Production: Inside the AWS x UTS Agentic AI Workshop
content:
DigiSAS Lab @ UTS — April 2026

A few weeks ago, the DigiSAS Lab team — staff and researchers from the School of Computer Science, Faculty of Engineering and IT — spent a day at Amazon Web Services (AWS) for an intensive Agentic AI Workshop, organised by A/Prof Asif Gill, Head of Discipline (Software Systems) and Director of the DigiSAS Lab, in collaboration with AWS.

The workshop was part of an ongoing effort to advance workforce capability development and the design of a Scalable Augmented Intelligence Architecture Layer — two foundational pillars of a modern AI Operating Model.

Not a Demo Day

This wasn’t a session of polished slideware or canned demonstrations. The team worked end-to-end — from core concepts and intelligence architecture patterns through to fully deployed, production-ready AI agents — all within a single day.

The focus was deliberately practical: how do we design human–AI agents that can:

  • reason across multiple steps,
  • use external tools,
  • retain short- and long-term context, and
  • integrate securely with enterprise systems on scalable, observable infrastructure?

Use Case: AI in Higher Education

The anchoring use case for the day was AI in Higher Education — a domain where human-centricity, trust, and ethical grounding are non-negotiable. This is the first in a planned series; upcoming workshops will extend the same architectural approach to Financial Services, Government, and Healthcare.

The Intelligence Architecture Layer

A central theme was the Intelligence Architecture Layer, structured around three capabilities:

  • Perception — how agents sense and ingest context
  • Thinking — how they reason, plan and decide
  • Action — how they execute, with tools and guardrails

This framing comes from A/Prof Gill’s forthcoming book, Architecting Human-Centric AI Systems – Augmented Intelligence (Gill, 2026).

The AWS Technology Stack

The team built on a rich AWS-native stack, including:

  • Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
  • Strands Agents SDK with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Kiro
  • Short- and long-term memory patterns
  • CloudWatch for monitoring and observability
  • IAM-based identity controls for secure, governed deployments

Together, these gave the team a concrete blueprint for taking agentic systems from prototype to production with the operational rigour enterprise environments demand.

Thank You

A huge thank you to Adrian Tadros, Daniela Miličević, Justin Brien and the broader AWS team for hosting and supporting such a productive day — and to the DigiSAS Lab researchers who took part: Dr Nabin Sharma, Madhushi Bandara, Yining Hu, Ali Braytee, Grace Billiris, Eesha Oaj, Bushra Sulayim and others.

What’s Next

DigiSAS Lab’s R&D agenda continues to focus on architecting and building human-centric, scalable Agentic AI systems — adaptable, observable, and ethically grounded by design. We’re looking forward to deepening collaboration with industry partners on workforce development and bringing Agentic AI to life, from concept to production.

If your organisation is interested in collaborating on research and development for an Intelligence Architecture Layer, get in touch with A/Prof Asif Gill at asif.gill@uts.edu.au.

title: DigiSAS Lab Workshop with A/Professor Sebastion Pies: Human-Centred AI Product Design
content:
DigiSAS Lab, UTS has invited Assistant Professor Sebastian Pies, from University of Twente, Neatherlands, to deliver a workshop on “Human-centred AI product design”

Details

When: 11th of August, 11-2pm

Where: School of Computer Science, UTS

Register Here

Workshop Abstract

Designing AI-enabled applications that genuinely augment human capabilities requires more than selecting the right machine learning techniques. It needs a human-centred design process that integrates perspectives from software engineering, artificial intelligence, human-computer interaction, information systems and domain experts.

In this interactive three-hour design workshop, Sebastian Piest shares practical tools and methods developed through his research to apply a structured, human-centred approach to designing and evaluating AI-enabled products. Participants are introduced to the Intelligence Amplification Design Method (IADM) and its central design tool, the Intelligence Amplification Design Canvas (IADC). The IADC supports the early-stage design and evaluation of human-centred AI products by structuring discussions around 13 design elements, organised according to four design principles.

Participants will work individually, in pairs or small groups to either develop a novel AI-application or analyse and improve an existing one. Through four design iteratations, participants will use the IADC to emphasize and define human-centred design aspects, the embodiment of AI as a software agent, the (potential) use of data driven approaches and computational intelligence, and incorporation of appropriate human in the loop interaction. Alongside the paper-based IADC, participants can experiment with the IA Co-designer, a custom GPT that supports AI-assisted design and reflection throughout the workshop.

By the end of the workshop, participants gained practical experience applying the IADC and IADM, a structured approach for designing and evaluating human-centred AI systems, and a concrete design concept or analysis that can serve as the foundation for future research or development.

title: Research Seminar by A/Professor Sebastion Pies
content:
AI-BOK: Towards an Integrated Enterprise Architecture for AI Governance

Following a successful interactive workshop, we are excited to invite Assistant Professor Sebastian Pies, from University of Twente, Neatherlands, to deliver a research seminar on “AI-BOK: Towards an Integrated Enterprise Architecture for AI Governance”

Details

When: 18th of August, 12-1pm

Where: CB11.06.408_FEITSeminarRoom, School of Computer Science, UTS (FEIT Building 11) and Online

Abstract

As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes an operational enterprise capability, organisations face a growing governance challenge. Standards and frameworks such as ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, TOGAF, and DAMA-DMBOK each address important aspects of AI management, risk, compliance, architecture, or data governance. However, organisations still need to integrate these perspectives into a coherent operating model that connects governance knowledge, organisational responsibilities, lifecycle activities, architecture, and regulatory obligations.

This seminar presents recent research on the AI Body of Knowledge (AI-BOK), an integrated reference framework for enterprise AI governance developed using a design science research approach. AI-BOK structures the domain into thirteen knowledge areas, twenty organisational roles, four governance bodies, an eight-phase AI lifecycle, and an ArchiMate-based reference architecture, while providing explicit mappings to established governance and architecture frameworks.

Particular attention will be given to the framework’s main conceptual contribution: the cognition plane, a proposed architectural construct for governing agentic AI. The cognition plane makes agent mandates, reasoning boundaries, delegation, grounding, composition constraints, and escalation explicit architectural concerns. We will examine why increasingly autonomous AI systems may challenge conventional enterprise architecture constructs, discuss the initial evaluation of AI-BOK with practitioners and academic experts, and consider the framework’s limitations and open research questions for advancement of AI-BOK within the FGEA CoP. The seminar concludes with a discussion of whether enterprise architecture needs new concepts to govern organisations in which both humans and autonomous AI agents exercise decision-making authority.

About the Speaker

Dr. J.P.S. (Sebastian) Piest is currently Assistant Professor and DesignLab Research Fellow at the University of Twente. He’s visiting the UTS DigiSAS Lab to collaborate on research regarding the design and architecture of human-centric AI systems, dataspaces and digital ecosystems and bringing the FGEA CoP to the Netherlands andEurope. title: DigiSAS Lab Seminar with Professor Patrick Mikalef: Agentic AI in the Wild: Delegation, Governance, and the Work That Stays Human
content:
DigiSAS Lab, UTS hosted Professor Patrick Mikalef, from Norwegian University of Science and Technology, to deliver an in-person seminar on “Agentic AI in the Wild: Delegation, Governance, and the Work That Stays Human.”

Details

When: Tuesday 25th August 11am – 12 noon

Where: CB11.06.408_FEITSeminarRoom, School of Computer Science, UTS (FEIT Building 11)

Talk Abstract

Agentic AI is a topic widely discussed and rarely observed. This talk reports one year of real use looks like inside one software development company. Where algorithmic management delegates managerial functions to systems from above, agentic systems let workers hand portions of their own tasks to software mid-task, in real time, while remaining answerable for whatever comes back. That inversion changes the work in ways the current literature does not anticipate. Drawing on a two-wave field study of a team that adopted coding agents early and now runs much of its work through them, we show what workers build around the technology to make delegation survivable, what happens to their position when they direct a system they must also answer for, and which work they refuse to hand over no matter how capable the agent becomes. The talk draws implications on information systems research, human resource management, and organizational governance in the age of agentic AI.

About the Speaker

Patrick Mikalef is Professor of Information Systems at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and Senior Research Scientist at SINTEF Digital. His research focuses on artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and responsible AI governance, with particular attention to how organisations develop the capabilities needed to generate strategic and societal value from advanced digital technologies. Patrick has published more than 200 peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings, including work in the European Journal of Information Systems, Journal of the Association for Information Systems, British Journal of Management, Information & Management, Decision Support Systems, and Journal of Strategic Information Systems. His research has received more than 30,000 citations, and he has been recognised as a Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher. He has led and contributed to several European and national research projects, including Horizon Europe and Marie Skłodowska-Curie initiatives, and is part of the leadership group of the Norwegian national research centre AI for Decisions. He regularly collaborates with industry and government organisations across Europe.

content:

The workshop introduced the concept of an Executable Twin: a structured representation of an organisation’s structure, knowledge and authorised actions, providing AI agents with the context and boundaries needed to operate responsibly.

Key Takeaways

1. Organisational Modelling for AI: Representing organisational structures, knowledge and processes to provide AI agents with the context needed to act.

3. Governing Agent Actions: Establishing clear organisational boundaries and authorised actions to support safe, accountable and governed agentic AI.

The workshop brought together perspectives on agentic AI, enterprise architecture, Digital Twins and AI governance, highlighting the importance of organisational context in enabling responsible AI adoption.

title: DigiSAS Lab Seminar with Dr Nassim Belbaly: Safe and Private by Design
content:
DigiSAS Lab, UTS has invited Dr Nassim Belbaly, Industry Liaison Lead at Western Sydney University, to deliver a mixed mode seminar on “Safe and Private by Design.”

Details

When: 24th of November 2026, 11am-12pm

Where: mixed mode, UTS

Talk Abstract

As AI systems become more capable and widely deployed, ensuring they behave safely and respect the people whose data they learn from has become a central challenge.

This talk explores three interconnected areas: AI safety, AI-enabled digital twins and privacy. The first part provides an overview of AI safety, examining challenges such as misaligned objectives, reward hacking, misuse and unreliable behaviour in high-stakes settings, alongside emerging approaches to alignment, interpretability and evaluation.

The second part explores these challenges through AI-enabled digital twins, drawing on research into emergency department optimisation with Liverpool Hospital and the Ingham Institute. It considers what safe deployment means when AI models inform decisions about patient flow and hospital resources, with a focus on validation, explainability and human oversight.

The final part examines privacy through AI-based anthropometry, where models estimate body measurements from images, scans and other sensor data. Using body data as an example, the talk highlights privacy risks such as re-identification and unintended inference, alongside privacy-preserving approaches. The session concludes with open research challenges and lessons for those building AI systems that process human data.

About the Speaker

Dr Nassim Belbaly is Industry Liaison Lead in the School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences at Western Sydney University, where he leads applied AI and digital twin research in collaboration with industry and healthcare partners, including Liverpool Hospital and the Ingham Institute. His research spans AI safety governance, AI-enabled monitoring and digital twins for emergency department optimisation.

With almost 20 years of academic leadership experience across Australia, the United Kingdom and France, Dr Belbaly has previously served as Dean of Birmingham City Business School and Dean of Academic Affairs at Montpellier Business School. His research has appeared in leading journals, including MIS Quarterly Executive, Technological Forecasting & Social Change and the International Journal of Information Management. He is also General Manager of Dragoai, an AI strategy and LLM solutions company.

title: Research Frontiers in Agentic AI, Data & Secure Digital Innovation
content:
In a new DigiSAS Lab Research Innovation Talk, Professor Asif Gill speaks with University of Technology Sydney researchers Grace Billiris, Eesha Oaj and Chuojun (Cecilia) Zhang about how agentic AI can support continuous privacy risk assessment, living business architecture and adaptive identity-fraud controls.

“We are not replacing humans. We are using agents to help humans. The message is about human augmentation”

Professor Asif Gill

Key takeaways from the discussion:

  • Context is essential for meaningful privacy-risk assessment
    Grace Billiris explains why the same data can carry very different privacy risks depending on its context. Her CAPRA framework and reference architecture use the phases Federate, Contextualise, Assess and Adapt to support continuous privacy-risk assessment across changing agentic AI systems.
  • Agentic AI can shift business architecture from static to living
    Eesha Oaj presents a Business Architecture Copilot that uses layered agents to model capabilities, assess their health and support evidence-based decisions. A shared knowledge base keeps architecture artefacts current while ensuring that architects retain the final judgement.
  • Multi-agent teams can strengthen identity-fraud controls
    Chuojun (Cecilia) Zhang describes an agent team that gathers evidence for identity-fraud investigations and adapts to emerging fraud techniques. Human investigators remain accountable for decisions, while evidence traceability helps people understand and trust the system’s outputs.
  • Human accountability remains central
    Across all three projects, AI agents augment rather than replace professionals. Strong data foundations, observable system behaviour, evidence traceability, privacy and security by design, and explicit human oversight are essential for trustworthy adoption.

Professor Gill concludes that the future of trustworthy AI depends on intentionally designed systems that strengthen human judgement and deliver value for organisations and the public good.

title: Business Architecture Copilot
content:
Partners: DigiSAS Lab (University of Technology Sydney) & Capsifi Pvt. Ltd 

2024-2028

Team:

Professor Asif Gill, Project Lead

Dr Madhushi Bandara, Co-Chief Investigator

Dr Terry Roach, Industry Partner/Investigator

Eesha Oaj, PhD student

Overview:

Business Architecture (BA) and plays a significant role in Business/IT alignment. Current methods in BA artefact generation and maintenance are largely manual, static, and time-consuming, which limits their effectiveness in dynamic and complex decision-making environments. Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased their potential in automating the generation of BA artefacts through customized prompting techniques. However, they face a key challenge due to the tendency of LLMs to hallucinate, resulting in outputs that may be inaccurate or inconsistent. Agentic AI offers an alternative approach for LLM based BA modelling, due to its ability to make autonomous decisions, adapt through learning, and process data in real time. To investigate their potential, this research project proposes Business Architecture Copilot: an Agentic AI-enabled business capability modelling approach that leverage AI agents to automate the generation of business capability maps. Our work employs an agentic system, implemented using the AutoGen 0.2 framework, integrated with an Enterprise Knowledge Graph (EKG) to semantically contextualise organisational knowledge. The proposed system enables AI agents to extract, reason over, and organise business capabilities, producing capability maps as the core artefact. The key outcomes of this research project are the Agentic AI-enabled Capability Modelling Architecture (AACMA) and an agent-based BA modelling process, designed to enhance decision-making in modern enterprise contexts.

content:
Enterprise Architecture for Augmented Intelligence (EA4AI) Workshop

The 1st International workshop on Enterprise Architecture for Augmented Intelligence (EA4AI)

In conjunction with CBI-EDOC 2025, September 09, 2025, Lisbon, Portugal.

About

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems seem to replicate or mimic human capabilities. There is an increasing interest in adopting such intelligent software systems for operational efficiency and innovation. While, interest is there, however, there is also fear among individuals or workforce that these intelligent software systems will replace human and their jobs, which may result in job losses and adverse impacts on society. We should not fear and shift our focus from traditional AI to human-centric augmented intelligence. Augmented intelligence goes beyond human capability replication or automation with a view to further enhance, or augment human capabilities.

Isolated or individual AI applications, models, proof-of-concepts (PoCs) and protype developments often fail to integrate with or scale at the enterprise level as production ready enterprise systems. For instance, how applications and models will share data with each other? How to ensure that models have controlled access to the right data based on their permission or need to know basis? How to avoid vendor lock-in where enterprise depend on different agents developed or provided by different service providers across the heterogeneous multi-cloud and on premises computing environment? How to ensure communication and coordination across such heterogeneous multi-agent AI systems? How to orchestrate, operate and manage such multi-agent environment at the enterprise and federated ecosystem levels.

The 1st International Workshop focuses on the challenge of “Scalable Enterprise AI” and proposes the Enterprise Architecture for Augmented Intelligence (EAAI). This workshop, as a part of the CBI-EDOC 2025 conference, aims at providing a forum to leading computer science researchers, enterprise architects, solution designers and practitioners to discuss the human-centric enterprise architecture methods, tools and techniques for architecting, building and deploying enterprise scale AI systems.

Keynote Abstract

Generative AI is shifting enterprise transformation beyond traditional automation toward augmentation, collaboration, and increasingly autonomous forms of agency. This keynote frames this transition as the emergence of a new agentic enterprise ecosystem, where humans, AI agents, intelligent services, data resources, workflows, governance mechanisms, and organisational goals interact dynamically to co-create value. Building on the vision of Agentic Service-Oriented Computing, the talk argues that future enterprise systems will no longer treat services as passive software components, but as intelligent, goal-directed, and collaborative actors capable of reasoning, coordination, adaptation, and responsible action. The keynote will explore how Enterprise Architecture must evolve to support these human-centric GenAI ecosystems through scalable architectural principles, governance models, trust mechanisms, and socio-technical design patterns. It will show how organisations can move from fragmented GenAI pilots to resilient agentic enterprises, where automation improves efficiency, augmentation strengthens human capability, and agency enables adaptive, responsible, and value-driven digital transformation.

Alongside his teaching and leadership roles, he has made significant contributions to applied artificial intelligence and data science research, securing more than 70 research projects and over $50 million in research funding. title: FGEA CoP
content:
Future Generation Enterprise Architecture (FGEA) Community of Practice (CoP)

Overview

Future Generation Enterprise Architecture (FGEA) Community of Practice (CoP) is based at the DigiSAS Lab, School of Computer Science, University of Technology Sydney (UTS). It provides a platform to EA practitioners, researchers and thought leaders from government, higher education and industry to exchange innovative ideas and best practices for architecting and building human-centric AI, data and digital ecosystems.

Purpose: Architecture for Public Good

Participation in the FGEA CoP is voluntary and by invitation based on the relevance to the enterprise architecture discipline and practice. The main purpose of the CoP is knowledge sharing, professional development, and capacity building in modern human-centric AI, Data & Digital Enterprise Systems & Architecture landscape for public good across different ecosystems with a view to explore the emerging trustworthy technologies, cyber, digital, data, AI/Gen AI adoptions, their threats and opportunities. This also includes developing professionals and future leaders in the overall spirit of UN’s SDG Goals, AI, Data & Digital Profession.

Structure

The FGEA CoP structure is organised as follows. General chair will provide the overall leadership and steering of the CoP. Convenor will provide the communication and coordination support across the CoP stakeholders. Advisory panel will provide the local and international perspectives and guidance across the CoP. There are three advisory committees, which will be led by the respective chairs and supported by the advisory committee members. Advisory committee chairs help setting and leading the agenda and round table discussions during the CoP sessions/symposiums. Advisory committee members propose topics and present at the CoP sessions/symposiums in consultation with the the chairs.

Global Data & Digital Alliance

Purpose

The DigiSAS Lab for Data & Digital (University of Technology Sydney), in collaboration with its core partners Fintech AI Innovation Consortium (University of New South Wales), and Applied AI Centre (Macquarie University), and associate Australian and International Universities established the Global Data & Digital Alliance (GDDA).  The GDDA brings together relevant global expertise from Academia, Government, and Industry to undertake cutting-edge applied research and develop high-tech exceptionally skilled data and digital workforce. 

Our Focus

The Alliance will focus on addressing the following major challenges to government, industry, and society:

  • How to co-design and deploy, trusted and secure, data & digital architectures for inclusive, ethical, and responsible, use of AI/GAI systems and services for all people and business?
  • How to evaluate the impact of data and digital on government, industry, and society?
  • How to build and evolve data and digital security and privacy in the context of AI/GAI?
  • How to manage and govern connected and federated data and digital assets? 
  • How to enable observability and semantic lineage in complex data and digital ecosystems?

title: Research & Innovation
content:
Digital Ecosystems

“Digital ecosystem (DE) is a dynamic configuration of informational organisms, individual and organisational actors, which interact in the digitally networked and federated environment”.

Gill, A.Q. (2022). The digital ecosystem information framework: Insights from action design research. Journal of Information Science, Sage Publication.

DigiSAS work is mainly concerned with the research and development of human-centric software and societal systems (S3) for the connected and complex data-intensive digital ecosystem (DE) that deal with the significant humanity and societal challenges.

Information (Data) is a foundation for digital innovation and transformation. DigiSAS focuses on strategic planning, architecture, and solutions underpinning software and societal systems (S3) for data-intensive digital ecosystems.

DigiSAS research is largely undertaken in collaboration with industry partners through research and innovation development contracts and internships. Research and innovation results are disseminated through industry short courses, workshops, seminars, forums, showcases, conferences, white papers and academic articles.

Software and Societal Systems (S3)

DigiSAS lab’s current work is organised into following three integrated areas of cybersecurity , data management and software systems within the broader area of human-centred software technology and solutions.

Public and private sector organisations are invited to team-up and collaborate with the DigiSAS Lab for exploring and addressing complex challenges of mutual interest for humanity and society.

Research Project Highlights*

Embedding Trust in Digital IDs for Consumers

Leader: Professor Asif Gill
Funding: UTS Central Research Budget (Grant; Jan 2025 – Dec 2026)
Description: Developing a trust-enhancing framework for digital identity systems, empowering consumers with stronger security and reliability when managing digital IDs.

Read More

Blockchain & Distributed Ledger Tokenisation

Leader: Professor Asif Gill
Funding: Digital Finance CRC Scholarship (Scholarship; Jul 2024 – Jun 2027)
Description: Scholarship-supported initiative exploring blockchain tokenisation approaches to improve transparency, efficiency, and trust in digital financial infrastructure.

Read More

Anti‑Cheat System for Chess

Leader: Associate Professor Nabin Sharma
Funding: Contract Research (Feb 2024 – Oct 2024)
Description: Develops AI-driven tools to detect and prevent cheating in online chess platforms through pattern recognition and behavioral analysis.

Read More

Future-Generation Digital Identity Management (“Data Zoo”)

Leader: Professor Asif Gill
Funding: Scholarship (Feb 2023 – Feb 2026)
Description: Innovates new digital identity paradigms—“Data Zoo”—focusing on privacy, interoperability, and user-centric identity ecosystems.

Read More

Evaluating and quantifying the benefits offered by a new virtual model of care for people requiring regular health services

Leader: Professor Asif Gill and Dr. Yanjun Zhang
Funding: Grant Digital Health CRC (Grant; Sep 2025 – Sep 2026)
Description: The CARED platform is an innovative model of care which combines telemonitoring, telehealth and home visits to empower users with dynamic on-demand care, solving many of the problems and frustrations associated with traditional models of care. This project will assess the technical design, functionality and performance of the CARED digital solution, and key dimensions of digital trust including cybersecurity, interoperability and privacy.

Read More

Understanding Healthcare Utilisation in Older Cancer Patients

Leader: Dr Madhushi Bandara
Funding: UTS Grant (Aug 2023 – Dec 2023)
Description: Investigates patterns of healthcare access and utilisation among older cancer patients to inform improvements in palliative and supportive care services.

Read More

Quality Assessment of Enterprise Knowledge Graphs

Leaders: Professors Asif Gill & Madhushi Bandara
Funding: Scholarship (Jan 2024 – Jul 2027)
Description: Evaluates and enhances the integrity, usability, and architecture of enterprise knowledge graphs to support scalable enterprise architecture.

Read More

Using XAI, NLP and Knowledge Graphs to Support Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence

Supervisors: Dr. Madhushi Bandara, Professor Asif Gill & A/Professor Catarina Pinto Moreira
Description: Explores the integration of explainable AI, natural language processing, and knowledge graphs to enhance the interpretability, accessibility, and scalability of AI systems, fostering trust and adoption in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity.

DAIRNet – AI for Decision Making & Drone Innovation

Leader: Associate Professor Nabin Sharma
Funding: Grant (May 2022 – Jul 2022)
Description: Applies Sequential Monte Carlo methods within DAIRNet to support informed decision-making in AI-powered drone systems.

Read More

Data Governance Framework for SMEs: Leveraging Knowledge-Graph

Supervisors: Dr. Madhushi Bandara & Professor Ghassan Beydoun
Description: Designs a lightweight, knowledge-graph-based data governance framework tailored for SMEs to improve data quality, accountability, and compliance while remaining cost-effective and scalable.

title: SEAD 2021
content:
Online Secure Enterprise Architecture Design (SEAD) Workshop

The 1st SEAD workshop is organized in conjunction with IEEE EDOC 2021, October 25, 2021, Gold Coast, Australia.

Please see below the the program and zoom link for joining the sessions.

Online Workshop SEAD 2021 Program, 25th October 2021

Zoom Link: https://zoom.uts.edu.au/j/87412812029

Brisbane, Australia Time

About

Traditional and isolated approaches to enterprise architecture, security and privacy often fall short. The 1st International Workshop focuses on secure enterprise architecture design (SEAD).  This workshop aims at providing a forum to government and industry who are interested in human-centric, performance outcome, risk-driven, data-driven and ecosystem-oriented approaches that are required to design the secure and adaptive enterprises. SEAD 2021 seeks experience reports, case studies and empirical research presentations including hands-on practical exercises or sessions that discuss the application of Enterprise Architecture and Security by Design practices in the real context. This provides opportunities to professionals and thought leaders to share, network and learn from each other through the presentation of industry success and failure cases. Government and Industry Practice Workshop will provide important insights into future directions and share practices which worked and which did not work including lessons learned, benefit realisation and limitations of SEAD practices. Government and industry submissions should be based on actual practice, and should cover all sides of the story – strengths and weaknesses, successes and challenges relevant to Enterprise Architecture and Security by Design practices.

Topics

Themes and topics of interest include, but are not limited to, the following:

Theme 1: Enterprise architecture

  • Human-centric CX architecture
  • Business architecture
  • Information architecture
  • Technology architecture
  • Performance architecture

Theme 2: Security architecture

  • Digital ethics and trust
  • Digital identity and access control
  • Digital forensics
  • Privacy by design
  • Peer-to-peer security
  • Security by design
  • Secure blockchain
  • Secure cloud
  • Secure IoT
  • Secure information management
  • Secure mobility

Submission Instructions

  • Prospective presenters are invited to submit an abstract (500-1000 words approximately), which outlines the proposed presentation or hands-on practical session with some key takeaways; additional material such as proposed slides or paper may also be submitted. All government and industry submissions will be reviewed by the program committee.
  • Authors of accepted submissions should then provide the intended presentation slides and/or a paper (8-10 pages full paper or 4 pages short paper) detailing the contents of the case study presentation.  Papers will be submitted for further review and publishing in the Enterprise Architecture Professional Journal (https://eapj.org/journal/). A “permission to publish” form will need to be signed by the authors or their organizations. One author from each accepted submission is required to register as a delegate and present at the workshop.
  • All papers must be original and not simultaneously submitted to another journal or conference. Papers should follow the example published (https://eapj.org/papers/) paper from Enterprise Architecture Professional Journal and be submitted in PDF format. Submissions must be in English and must not exceed the above-mentioned limit pages (including abstract, figures and references).

Submission System

  • Abstract and paper (PDF) must be submitted electronically via the Workshop Submission System: Please click here to submit via Easy Access Conference System

Important Dates

  • Workshop abstract submission: 30 August 2021
  • Workshop acceptance notification: 13 September 2021
  • Workshop papers and presentations due: 27 September 2021
  • Author registration: 27 September 2021
  • Workshops sessions: 25 October 2020
